Databases.front: What is a database index intersection?
Databases.easy: It helps you learn about database.
Databases.normal: Index intersection uses multiple indexes. PostgreSQL can combine bitmap scans. MySQL also supports index merge. Alternative to multi-column index when creating.
Databases.hard: Index intersection uses multiple indexes to satisfy a query (Bitmap AND/OR). PostgreSQL can combine bitmap scans from different indexes. MySQL also supports index merge. Alternative to multi-column index when creating separate indexes.
Databases.expert: Index intersection uses multiple indexes to satisfy a query (Bitmap AND/OR). PostgreSQL can combine bitmap scans from different indexes. MySQL also supports index merge. Alternative to multi-column index when creating separate indexes. Choose based on your specific requirements.

Databases.easy: It helps you learn about database.
Databases.normal: pg_hint_plan extension forces specific query plans. Useful when planner chooses suboptimal plan. Example: /*+ SeqScant */ SELECT *. Last resort; maintain statistics first.
Databases.hard: pg_hint_plan extension forces specific query plans using hints embedded in comments. Useful when planner chooses suboptimal plan due to stale statistics. Example: /*+ SeqScan(t) */ SELECT * FROM t. Last resort; maintain statistics first.
Databases.expert: pg_hint_plan extension forces specific query plans using hints embedded in comments. Useful when planner chooses suboptimal plan due to stale statistics. Example: /*+ SeqScan(t) */ SELECT * FROM t. Last resort; maintain statistics first. Evaluate trade-offs before deciding.

Databases.front: How does PostgreSQL handle JSONB indexing?
Databases.easy: It helps you learn about PostgreSQL.
Databases.normal: JSONB supports GIN index for @>. Path-specific index via jsonb_path_ops (smaller faster). Also B-Tree on entire JSONB. Supports expression indexes on extracted fields. Better performance than JSON (text) type.
Databases.hard: JSONB supports GIN index for @>, ?, ?|, ?& operators. Path-specific index via jsonb_path_ops (smaller faster). Also B-Tree on entire JSONB. Supports expression indexes on extracted fields. Better performance than JSON (text) type.
Databases.expert: JSONB supports GIN index for @>, ?, ?|, ?& operators. Path-specific index via jsonb_path_ops (smaller faster). Also B-Tree on entire JSONB. Supports expression indexes on extracted fields. Better performance than JSON (text) type. Context determines the best approach.

Databases.front: What is a database index skip scan?
Databases.easy: It helps you learn about database.
Databases.normal: Skip scan allows searching without leftmost. MySQL 8.0+ supports skip scan natively. Avoids full index scan for queries.
Databases.hard: Skip scan allows searching without leftmost index column (PostgreSQL implements via recursive CTE or multiple index scans). MySQL 8.0+ supports skip scan natively. Avoids full index scan for queries missing prefix columns.
Databases.expert: Skip scan allows searching without leftmost index column (PostgreSQL implements via recursive CTE or multiple index scans). MySQL 8.0+ supports skip scan natively. Avoids full index scan for queries missing prefix columns. Evaluate trade-offs before deciding.

Databases.front: What is SQL injection and how to prevent it?
Databases.easy: It helps you learn about injection.
Databases.normal: SQL injection occurs when user input. Prevention: parameterized queries prepared statements, input. Never trust user input in raw.
Databases.hard: SQL injection occurs when user input is concatenated into SQL queries. Prevention: parameterized queries (prepared statements), input validation, ORM usage, least privilege database user, and stored procedures. Never trust user input in raw SQL strings.
Databases.expert: SQL injection occurs when user input is concatenated into SQL queries. Prevention: parameterized queries (prepared statements), input validation, ORM usage, least privilege database user, and stored procedures. Never trust user input in raw SQL strings. Consider performance and maintainability.

System Design.front: Explain how DNS resolution works end-to-end.
System Design.easy: It helps you learn about resolution.
System Design.normal: Browser checks local cache, then OS. Resolver queries root nameserver for TLD. Response chain cached at each level.
System Design.hard: Browser checks local cache, then OS resolver queries recursive resolver. Resolver queries root nameserver for TLD NS, then TLD nameserver for authoritative NS, then authoritative server for IP. Response chain cached at each level with TTL.
System Design.expert: Browser checks local cache, then OS resolver queries recursive resolver. Resolver queries root nameserver for TLD NS, then TLD nameserver for authoritative NS, then authoritative server for IP. Response chain cached at each level with TTL. Choose based on your specific requirements.

System Design.front: What is CDN and how does it improve performance?
System Design.easy: It helps you learn about improve.
System Design.normal: CDN Content Delivery Network caches static. Reduces latency, offloads origin servers. Uses Anycast routing to direct users. Common: CloudFront, Cloudflare, Akamai.
System Design.hard: CDN (Content Delivery Network) caches static content at edge servers geographically closer to users. Reduces latency, offloads origin servers. Uses Anycast routing to direct users to nearest PoP. Common: CloudFront, Cloudflare, Akamai.
System Design.expert: CDN (Content Delivery Network) caches static content at edge servers geographically closer to users. Reduces latency, offloads origin servers. Uses Anycast routing to direct users to nearest PoP. Common: CloudFront, Cloudflare, Akamai. Choose based on your specific requirements.

System Design.front: Explain load balancing algorithms.
System Design.easy: It helps you learn about load.
System Design.normal: Round Robin: sequential distribution. Least Connections: sends to least loaded. IP Hash: consistent routing same client. Weighted: distributes proportionally by capacity. Random: simple but uneven. Health checks required.
System Design.hard: Round Robin: sequential distribution. Least Connections: sends to least loaded server. IP Hash: consistent routing same client to same server. Weighted: distributes proportionally by capacity. Random: simple but uneven. Health checks required.
System Design.expert: Round Robin: sequential distribution. Least Connections: sends to least loaded server. IP Hash: consistent routing same client to same server. Weighted: distributes proportionally by capacity. Random: simple but uneven. Health checks required. Consider performance and maintainability.

System Design.front: How does consistent hashing work for distributed caching?
System Design.easy: It helps you learn about consistent.
System Design.normal: Maps keys and servers to unit. Each key assigned to next server. Adding/removing server only remaps keys. Minimizes cache misses on scaling. Used by DynamoDB, Cassandra, Memcached.
System Design.hard: Maps keys and servers to unit circle via hash function. Each key assigned to next server clockwise. Adding/removing server only remaps keys in adjacent range. Minimizes cache misses on scaling. Used by DynamoDB, Cassandra, Memcached.
System Design.expert: Maps keys and servers to unit circle via hash function. Each key assigned to next server clockwise. Adding/removing server only remaps keys in adjacent range. Minimizes cache misses on scaling. Used by DynamoDB, Cassandra, Memcached. Choose based on your specific requirements.

System Design.front: What is the difference between horizontal and vertical scaling?
System Design.easy: It helps you learn about difference.
System Design.normal: Horizontal scale out: add more machines. Vertical scale up: bigger machine, simpler. Modern systems favor horizontal.
System Design.hard: Horizontal (scale out): add more machines, better fault tolerance, requires load balancing and data distribution. Vertical (scale up): bigger machine, simpler but has hardware limits, single point of failure. Modern systems favor horizontal.
System Design.expert: Horizontal (scale out): add more machines, better fault tolerance, requires load balancing and data distribution. Vertical (scale up): bigger machine, simpler but has hardware limits, single point of failure. Modern systems favor horizontal. Consider performance and maintainability.

System Design.front: Explain database read replicas architecture.
System Design.easy: It helps you learn about database.
System Design.normal: Primary handles writes, replicas handle read. Reduces primary load, improves read throughput. Replication lag causes stale reads. Use cases: reporting, analytics, cache warming. Failover promotes replica to primary.
System Design.hard: Primary handles writes, replicas handle read queries asynchronously. Reduces primary load, improves read throughput. Replication lag causes stale reads. Use cases: reporting, analytics, cache warming. Failover promotes replica to primary.
System Design.expert: Primary handles writes, replicas handle read queries asynchronously. Reduces primary load, improves read throughput. Replication lag causes stale reads. Use cases: reporting, analytics, cache warming. Failover promotes replica to primary. Choose based on your specific requirements.

System Design.front: What is sharding and its challenges?
System Design.easy: It helps you learn about sharding.
System Design.normal: Sharding splits data across databases. Challenges: choosing good shard key, cross-shard. Solutions: proxy-based sharding (Vitess) or app-level.
System Design.hard: Sharding splits data across databases by shard key. Challenges: choosing good shard key, cross-shard queries (scatter-gather), resharding, backup complexity, transaction atomicity across shards. Solutions: proxy-based sharding (Vitess) or app-level.
System Design.expert: Sharding splits data across databases by shard key. Challenges: choosing good shard key, cross-shard queries (scatter-gather), resharding, backup complexity, transaction atomicity across shards. Solutions: proxy-based sharding (Vitess) or app-level. Evaluate trade-offs before deciding.

System Design.front: Explain the CAP theorem in practice.
System Design.easy: It helps you learn about theorem.
System Design.normal: CAP: Consistency, Availability, Partition tolerance pick. Network partition forces trade-off: CP Bank. Social media: AP. Modern DBs offer tunable consistency.
System Design.hard: CAP: Consistency, Availability, Partition tolerance pick 2. Network partition forces trade-off: CP (deny writes return errors) vs AP (accept writes may read stale). Bank: CP. Social media: AP. Modern DBs offer tunable consistency.
System Design.expert: CAP: Consistency, Availability, Partition tolerance pick 2. Network partition forces trade-off: CP (deny writes return errors) vs AP (accept writes may read stale). Bank: CP. Social media: AP. Modern DBs offer tunable consistency.

System Design.front: How does a message queue (Kafka/RabbitMQ) work?
System Design.easy: It helps you learn about message.
System Design.normal: Producers publish messages to topics/queues. Brokers store and replicate messages. Consumers subscribe and process. Kafka uses pull model with offset. RabbitMQ uses push with exchanges.
System Design.hard: Producers publish messages to topics/queues. Brokers store and replicate messages. Consumers subscribe and process. Kafka uses pull model with offset tracking, log-based storage, partitions for parallelism. RabbitMQ uses push with exchanges and bindings.
System Design.expert: Producers publish messages to topics/queues. Brokers store and replicate messages. Consumers subscribe and process. Kafka uses pull model with offset tracking, log-based storage, partitions for parallelism. RabbitMQ uses push with exchanges and bindings. Context determines the best approach.

System Design.front: What is circuit breaker pattern?
System Design.easy: It helps you learn about circuit.
System Design.normal: Protects system from cascading failures. Three states: Closed normal, Open. Transitions based on failure threshold.
System Design.hard: Protects system from cascading failures by stopping calls to failing service. Three states: Closed (normal), Open (fail fast immediately), Half-Open (test with limited calls after timeout). Transitions based on failure threshold and timeout.
System Design.expert: Protects system from cascading failures by stopping calls to failing service. Three states: Closed (normal), Open (fail fast immediately), Half-Open (test with limited calls after timeout). Transitions based on failure threshold and timeout. Choose based on your specific requirements.

System Design.front: Explain cache eviction strategies for system design.
System Design.easy: It helps you learn about cache.
System Design.normal: LRU : evicts oldest accessed item. LFU : evicts least accessed. FIFO: evicts oldest. TTL: expire by time. Redis uses LRU approximation (volatile-lru, allkeys-lru). Memcached uses LRU.
System Design.hard: LRU (Least Recently Used): evicts oldest accessed item. LFU (Least Frequently Used): evicts least accessed. FIFO: evicts oldest. TTL: expire by time. Redis uses LRU approximation (volatile-lru, allkeys-lru). Memcached uses LRU.
System Design.expert: LRU (Least Recently Used): evicts oldest accessed item. LFU (Least Frequently Used): evicts least accessed. FIFO: evicts oldest. TTL: expire by time. Redis uses LRU approximation (volatile-lru, allkeys-lru). Memcached uses LRU. Consider performance and maintainability.

System Design.front: How does a distributed rate limiter work?
System Design.easy: It helps you learn about distributed.
System Design.normal: Token bucket: tokens refill at rate. Sliding window: count requests in rolling. Distributed requires shared counter (Redis). Algorithm: sliding window log or sliding. Returns 429 Too Many Requests.
System Design.hard: Token bucket: tokens refill at rate per time window. Sliding window: count requests in rolling window. Distributed requires shared counter (Redis). Algorithm: sliding window log or sliding window counter. Returns 429 Too Many Requests.
System Design.expert: Token bucket: tokens refill at rate per time window. Sliding window: count requests in rolling window. Distributed requires shared counter (Redis). Algorithm: sliding window log or sliding window counter. Returns 429 Too Many Requests. Evaluate trade-offs before deciding.

System Design.front: What is two-phase commit (2PC) in distributed transactions?
System Design.easy: It helps you learn about phase.
System Design.normal: Phase 1 Prepare: coordinator asks all. Phase 2 Commit: if all yes. Blocking protocol coordinator failure blocks participants. Alternatives: Saga, TCC.
System Design.hard: Phase 1 (Prepare): coordinator asks all participants if they can commit. Phase 2 (Commit): if all yes, coordinator tells all to commit; if any no, abort. Blocking protocol coordinator failure blocks participants. Alternatives: Saga, TCC.
System Design.expert: Phase 1 (Prepare): coordinator asks all participants if they can commit. Phase 2 (Commit): if all yes, coordinator tells all to commit; if any no, abort. Blocking protocol coordinator failure blocks participants. Alternatives: Saga, TCC. Consider performance and maintainability.

System Design.front: Explain the Saga pattern for distributed transactions.
System Design.easy: It helps you learn about Saga.
System Design.normal: Saga decomposes long transaction into series. Choreography: each service publishes events triggering. Orchestration: coordinator tells services what. Each step has corresponding rollback.
System Design.hard: Saga decomposes long transaction into series of local transactions with compensating actions. Choreography: each service publishes events triggering next step. Orchestration: coordinator tells services what to do. Each step has corresponding rollback.
System Design.expert: Saga decomposes long transaction into series of local transactions with compensating actions. Choreography: each service publishes events triggering next step. Orchestration: coordinator tells services what to do. Each step has corresponding rollback. Context determines the best approach.

System Design.front: How does a distributed cache (Redis Cluster) work?
System Design.easy: It helps you learn about distributed.
System Design.normal: Redis Cluster uses hash slots . Keys mapped to slots via CRC16. Slots distributed across nodes. Nodes communicate via gossip protocol. Automatic failover with replicas. No central proxy; clients know slot-to-node.
System Design.hard: Redis Cluster uses hash slots (16384 total). Keys mapped to slots via CRC16. Slots distributed across nodes. Nodes communicate via gossip protocol. Automatic failover with replicas. No central proxy; clients know slot-to-node mapping.
System Design.expert: Redis Cluster uses hash slots (16384 total). Keys mapped to slots via CRC16. Slots distributed across nodes. Nodes communicate via gossip protocol. Automatic failover with replicas. No central proxy; clients know slot-to-node mapping. Choose based on your specific requirements.

System Design.front: What is Eventually Consistent model?
System Design.easy: It helps you learn about Eventually.
System Design.normal: After write stops, replicas converge. No guarantee of immediate consistency. Used by DNS, CDN, DynamoDB, Cassandra. Trade-off: higher availability and partition tolerance.
System Design.hard: After write stops, replicas converge to same value over time. No guarantee of immediate consistency. Used by DNS, CDN, DynamoDB, Cassandra. Trade-off: higher availability and partition tolerance for eventual consistency.
System Design.expert: After write stops, replicas converge to same value over time. No guarantee of immediate consistency. Used by DNS, CDN, DynamoDB, Cassandra. Trade-off: higher availability and partition tolerance for eventual consistency.

System Design.front: Explain how to design a URL shortener.
System Design.easy: It helps you learn about design.
System Design.normal: Key components: hash function base62, MD5/truncated. DB: bigint for ID, varchar. Handle collisions via retry or distributed.
System Design.hard: Key components: hash function (base62, MD5/truncated), key generation service (pre-generate unique IDs), redirect (301/302), analytics, rate limiting. DB: bigint for ID, varchar for URL. Handle collisions via retry or distributed ID (Snowflake).
System Design.expert: Key components: hash function (base62, MD5/truncated), key generation service (pre-generate unique IDs), redirect (301/302), analytics, rate limiting. DB: bigint for ID, varchar for URL. Handle collisions via retry or distributed ID (Snowflake). Choose based on your specific requirements.

System Design.front: How does WebSockets differ from HTTP polling?
System Design.easy: It helps you learn about WebSockets.
System Design.normal: WebSocket: full-duplex persistent connection over single. Low overhead . HTTP polling: client repeatedly polls server. WebSocket better for real-time apps .
System Design.hard: WebSocket: full-duplex persistent connection over single TCP socket. Low overhead (2 bytes per frame after upgrade). HTTP polling: client repeatedly polls server (high latency, overhead). WebSocket better for real-time apps (chat, notifications).
System Design.expert: WebSocket: full-duplex persistent connection over single TCP socket. Low overhead (2 bytes per frame after upgrade). HTTP polling: client repeatedly polls server (high latency, overhead). WebSocket better for real-time apps (chat, notifications). Choose based on your specific requirements.

System Design.front: What is the difference between REST and GraphQL?
System Design.easy: It helps you learn about difference.
System Design.normal: REST: fixed endpoints return predefined data. Multiple endpoints for different views. GraphQL: single endpoint, client specifies exact. Reduces over-fetching and under-fetching. Complex queries can overload server; need.
System Design.hard: REST: fixed endpoints return predefined data shapes. Multiple endpoints for different views. GraphQL: single endpoint, client specifies exact data needs. Reduces over-fetching and under-fetching. Complex queries can overload server; need depth limiting and cost analysis.
System Design.expert: REST: fixed endpoints return predefined data shapes. Multiple endpoints for different views. GraphQL: single endpoint, client specifies exact data needs. Reduces over-fetching and under-fetching. Complex queries can overload server; need depth limiting and cost analysis. Context determines the best approach.

System Design.front: Explain how to design a distributed ID generator.
System Design.easy: It helps you learn about design.
System Design.normal: Requirements: globally unique, roughly sortable, high. Approaches: UUID (128-bit, unsorted, large). Snowflake Twitter: timestamp + worker ID. Database sequence (bottleneck). Redis INCR (bottleneck). Snowflake common choice.
System Design.hard: Requirements: globally unique, roughly sortable, high throughput. Approaches: UUID (128-bit, unsorted, large). Snowflake (Twitter): timestamp + worker ID + sequence (64-bit). Database sequence (bottleneck). Redis INCR (bottleneck). Snowflake common choice.
System Design.expert: Requirements: globally unique, roughly sortable, high throughput. Approaches: UUID (128-bit, unsorted, large). Snowflake (Twitter): timestamp + worker ID + sequence (64-bit). Database sequence (bottleneck). Redis INCR (bottleneck). Snowflake common choice. Context determines the best approach.

System Design.front: How does a distributed file system (HDFS) work?
System Design.easy: It helps you learn about distributed.
System Design.normal: HDFS: NameNode manages metadata (file-to-block mapping). DataNodes store blocks . Write pipeline: client writes to first. Read: client gets block locations.
System Design.hard: HDFS: NameNode manages metadata (file-to-block mapping). DataNodes store blocks (default 128MB, replicated 3x). Write pipeline: client writes to first DataNode, forwarded to replicas. Read: client gets block locations from NameNode, reads from nearest DataNode.
System Design.expert: HDFS: NameNode manages metadata (file-to-block mapping). DataNodes store blocks (default 128MB, replicated 3x). Write pipeline: client writes to first DataNode, forwarded to replicas. Read: client gets block locations from NameNode, reads from nearest DataNode. Consider performance and maintainability.

System Design.front: What is leader election in distributed systems?
System Design.easy: It helps you learn about leader.
System Design.normal: Process of selecting one node. Algorithms: Raft , Paxos, Zab . Leader handles writes, manages consensus. Failure detection via heartbeats. Automatic re-election on leader failure.
System Design.hard: Process of selecting one node as leader for coordination. Algorithms: Raft (term-based, random timeout), Paxos, Zab (ZooKeeper). Leader handles writes, manages consensus. Failure detection via heartbeats. Automatic re-election on leader failure.
System Design.expert: Process of selecting one node as leader for coordination. Algorithms: Raft (term-based, random timeout), Paxos, Zab (ZooKeeper). Leader handles writes, manages consensus. Failure detection via heartbeats. Automatic re-election on leader failure. Evaluate trade-offs before deciding.

System Design.front: Explain how ZooKeeper works.
System Design.easy: It helps you learn about ZooKeeper.
System Design.normal: ZooKeeper provides distributed coordination primitives: ephemeral. Znode tree structure. Used for leader election, service discovery. Based on Zab protocol for atomic.
System Design.hard: ZooKeeper provides distributed coordination primitives: ephemeral nodes (session-scoped), sequential nodes, watches for notifications. Znode tree structure. Used for leader election, service discovery, configuration management. Based on Zab protocol for atomic broadcast.
System Design.expert: ZooKeeper provides distributed coordination primitives: ephemeral nodes (session-scoped), sequential nodes, watches for notifications. Znode tree structure. Used for leader election, service discovery, configuration management. Based on Zab protocol for atomic broadcast. Evaluate trade-offs before deciding.

System Design.front: How does a distributed lock work with Redis?
System Design.easy: It helps you learn about distributed.
System Design.normal: Redlock algorithm: acquire lock on majority. Each node has TTL. Client adds unique value. Release via Lua script checking value. Problems: clock drift, GC pauses. Simpler alternative: single Redis with TTL.
System Design.hard: Redlock algorithm: acquire lock on majority of N Redis nodes. Each node has TTL. Client adds unique value. Release via Lua script checking value. Problems: clock drift, GC pauses. Simpler alternative: single Redis with TTL and fencing tokens.
System Design.expert: Redlock algorithm: acquire lock on majority of N Redis nodes. Each node has TTL. Client adds unique value. Release via Lua script checking value. Problems: clock drift, GC pauses. Simpler alternative: single Redis with TTL and fencing tokens. Consider performance and maintainability.

System Design.front: What is the difference between TCP and UDP? When to use each?
System Design.easy: It helps you learn about difference.
System Design.normal: TCP: connection-oriented, guaranteed delivery, in-order, flow. Used for HTTP, SMTP, SSH. UDP: connectionless, no guarantees, low overhead. Used for DNS, VoIP, video streaming. Trade: reliability vs latency.
System Design.hard: TCP: connection-oriented, guaranteed delivery, in-order, flow control, congestion control. Used for HTTP, SMTP, SSH. UDP: connectionless, no guarantees, low overhead. Used for DNS, VoIP, video streaming, gaming. Trade: reliability vs latency.
System Design.expert: TCP: connection-oriented, guaranteed delivery, in-order, flow control, congestion control. Used for HTTP, SMTP, SSH. UDP: connectionless, no guarantees, low overhead. Used for DNS, VoIP, video streaming, gaming. Trade: reliability vs latency.

System Design.front: Explain how to design a chat system.
System Design.easy: It helps you learn about design.
System Design.normal: Components: connection handler WebSocket, message service. Architecture: fan-out on write. Cassandra for message store Channel-based pub/sub.
System Design.hard: Components: connection handler (WebSocket), message service, presence service, notification service, message store. Architecture: fan-out on write (pre-compute inbox for small groups) vs fan-out on read. Cassandra for message store. Channel-based pub/sub.
System Design.expert: Components: connection handler (WebSocket), message service, presence service, notification service, message store. Architecture: fan-out on write (pre-compute inbox for small groups) vs fan-out on read. Cassandra for message store. Channel-based pub/sub. Choose based on your specific requirements.

System Design.front: How does a distributed queue (Kafka) achieve high throughput?
System Design.easy: It helps you learn about distributed.
System Design.normal: Kafka uses: sequential disk I/O. Topic partitions enable parallelism. Consumer groups for horizontal scaling. Pages from OS page cache. Broker handles 100K+ msg/s per partition.
System Design.hard: Kafka uses: sequential disk I/O (append-only log), zero-copy (sendfile), batching, partitioning, compression. Topic partitions enable parallelism. Consumer groups for horizontal scaling. Pages from OS page cache for hot data. Broker handles 100K+ msg/s per partition.
System Design.expert: Kafka uses: sequential disk I/O (append-only log), zero-copy (sendfile), batching, partitioning, compression. Topic partitions enable parallelism. Consumer groups for horizontal scaling. Pages from OS page cache for hot data. Broker handles 100K+ msg/s per partition. Evaluate trade-offs before deciding.

System Design.front: What is a bloom filter and how is it used in system design?
System Design.easy: It helps you learn about bloom.
System Design.normal: Probabilistic data structure testing set membership. No false negatives, configurable false positives. Used in: CDN cache filtering. Reduces expensive lookups.
System Design.hard: Probabilistic data structure testing set membership. No false negatives, configurable false positives. Used in: CDN cache filtering (cache if bloom says cached), Cassandra (pre-check SSTable existence), Bitcoin SPV nodes, HBase. Reduces expensive lookups.
System Design.expert: Probabilistic data structure testing set membership. No false negatives, configurable false positives. Used in: CDN cache filtering (cache if bloom says cached), Cassandra (pre-check SSTable existence), Bitcoin SPV nodes, HBase. Reduces expensive lookups. Evaluate trade-offs before deciding.

System Design.front: Explain CQRS pattern.
System Design.easy: It helps you learn about CQRS.
System Design.normal: Command Query Responsibility Segregation: separate read. Commands writes use different model/DB than. Benefits: optimize each for workload, independent. Complexity: eventual consistency between models.
System Design.hard: Command Query Responsibility Segregation: separate read and write models. Commands (writes) use different model/DB than queries (reads). Benefits: optimize each for workload, independent scaling, separate security boundaries. Complexity: eventual consistency between models.
System Design.expert: Command Query Responsibility Segregation: separate read and write models. Commands (writes) use different model/DB than queries (reads). Benefits: optimize each for workload, independent scaling, separate security boundaries. Complexity: eventual consistency between models. Evaluate trade-offs before deciding.

System Design.front: How does Event Sourcing work?
System Design.easy: It helps you learn about Event.
System Design.normal: Stores all state changes as sequence. Current state = fold over events. Benefits: complete audit trail, time travel. Challenges: event schema evolution, querying current. Often paired with CQRS.
System Design.hard: Stores all state changes as sequence of events (append-only log). Current state = fold over events. Benefits: complete audit trail, time travel, event-driven integrations. Challenges: event schema evolution, querying current state requires replay. Often paired with CQRS.
System Design.expert: Stores all state changes as sequence of events (append-only log). Current state = fold over events. Benefits: complete audit trail, time travel, event-driven integrations. Challenges: event schema evolution, querying current state requires replay. Often paired with CQRS. Evaluate trade-offs before deciding.

System Design.front: What is a distributed tracing system (Jaeger/Zipkin)?
System Design.easy: It helps you learn about distributed.
System Design.normal: Tracing assigns each request a trace. Spans represent operations within the trace. Context propagated via headers (traceparent). Jaeger uses sampling strategies. Spans sent to collector, stored. UI shows waterfall view for latency.
System Design.hard: Tracing assigns each request a trace ID. Spans represent operations within the trace. Context propagated via headers (traceparent). Jaeger uses sampling strategies. Spans sent to collector, stored in Elasticsearch/Cassandra. UI shows waterfall view for latency analysis.
System Design.expert: Tracing assigns each request a trace ID. Spans represent operations within the trace. Context propagated via headers (traceparent). Jaeger uses sampling strategies. Spans sent to collector, stored in Elasticsearch/Cassandra. UI shows waterfall view for latency analysis. Evaluate trade-offs before deciding.

System Design.front: Explain how to design a rate limiter.
System Design.easy: It helps you learn about design.
System Design.normal: Components: rule storage, counter storage Redis. Algorithms: token bucket constant rate, leaky. Response: 429 status, Retry-After header.
System Design.hard: Components: rule storage, counter storage (Redis), algorithm selection. Algorithms: token bucket (constant rate), leaky bucket (smoothing), sliding window log (accurate), sliding window counter (efficient). Response: 429 status, Retry-After header.
System Design.expert: Components: rule storage, counter storage (Redis), algorithm selection. Algorithms: token bucket (constant rate), leaky bucket (smoothing), sliding window log (accurate), sliding window counter (efficient). Response: 429 status, Retry-After header. Evaluate trade-offs before deciding.

System Design.front: How does a search index (Elasticsearch) work?
System Design.easy: It helps you learn about search.
System Design.normal: Inverted index mapping terms to documents. Documents stored as JSON, indexed into. Query: tokenizes, looks up posting list. Distributed across nodes with replication. Near-real-time: refresh interval 1s default makes.
System Design.hard: Inverted index mapping terms to documents. Documents stored as JSON, indexed into shards. Query: tokenizes, looks up posting list, scores (BM25). Distributed across nodes with replication. Near-real-time: refresh interval (1s default) makes new docs searchable.
System Design.expert: Inverted index mapping terms to documents. Documents stored as JSON, indexed into shards. Query: tokenizes, looks up posting list, scores (BM25). Distributed across nodes with replication. Near-real-time: refresh interval (1s default) makes new docs searchable. Context determines the best approach.

System Design.front: What is a data lakehouse architecture?
System Design.easy: It helps you learn about data.
System Design.normal: Combines data lake flexibility. Delta Lake, Apache Iceberg, Apache Hudi. Databricks lakehouse prominent example.
System Design.hard: Combines data lake flexibility (cheap object storage, schema-on-read) with warehouse reliability (ACID, schema enforcement, performance optimizations). Delta Lake, Apache Iceberg, Apache Hudi provide ACID on Parquet/ORC files. Databricks lakehouse prominent example.
System Design.expert: Combines data lake flexibility (cheap object storage, schema-on-read) with warehouse reliability (ACID, schema enforcement, performance optimizations). Delta Lake, Apache Iceberg, Apache Hudi provide ACID on Parquet/ORC files. Databricks lakehouse prominent example. Context determines the best approach.

System Design.front: Explain how to design a payment system.
System Design.easy: It helps you learn about design.
System Design.normal: Components: payment gateway, payment processor, merchant. Idempotency key prevents duplicate charges. Two-phase commit-like: authorize then capture. Handle failures: retry with idempotency, compensate. Compliance: PCI-DSS, encryption, tokenization.

System Design.front: What is the difference between synchronous and asynchronous replication?
System Design.easy: It helps you learn about difference.
System Design.normal: Synchronous: write completes only when all. Strong consistency, higher latency, reduced write. Asynchronous: primary acknowledges without waiting. Better performance, risk of data loss. Trade: consistency vs performance.
System Design.hard: Synchronous: write completes only when all replicas acknowledge. Strong consistency, higher latency, reduced write availability. Asynchronous: primary acknowledges without waiting for replicas. Better performance, risk of data loss on failure. Trade: consistency vs performance.
System Design.expert: Synchronous: write completes only when all replicas acknowledge. Strong consistency, higher latency, reduced write availability. Asynchronous: primary acknowledges without waiting for replicas. Better performance, risk of data loss on failure. Trade: consistency vs performance.

System Design.easy: It helps you learn about Proxy.
System Design.normal: Forward proxy: client-side (filtering, caching, anonymity). Reverse proxy: server-side . Nginx, HAProxy, Envoy as reverse proxies. Placed between clients and servers.
System Design.hard: Forward proxy: client-side (filtering, caching, anonymity). Reverse proxy: server-side (load balancing, SSL termination, caching, compression). Nginx, HAProxy, Envoy as reverse proxies. Placed between clients and servers for abstraction.
System Design.expert: Forward proxy: client-side (filtering, caching, anonymity). Reverse proxy: server-side (load balancing, SSL termination, caching, compression). Nginx, HAProxy, Envoy as reverse proxies. Placed between clients and servers for abstraction. Context determines the best approach.

System Design.expert: Optimized for append-heavy write workload with time-ordering. Storage: LSM-tree (InfluxDB TSM), columnar (TimescaleDB hypertables). Downsampling: rollups at lower resolution. System Design.front: How does the Gossip protocol work?

System Design.normal: Each node periodically exchanges state. Information spreads exponentially (gossip fan-out). Eventually all nodes converge. Used in Cassandra, Dynamo, Consul. Efficient but eventual.
System Design.hard: Each node periodically exchanges state with random peers (P2P). Information spreads exponentially (gossip fan-out). Eventually all nodes converge. Used in Cassandra, Dynamo, Consul for failure detection, membership, metadata propagation. Efficient but eventual.
System Design.expert: Each node periodically exchanges state with random peers (P2P). Information spreads exponentially (gossip fan-out). Eventually all nodes converge. Used in Cassandra, Dynamo, Consul for failure detection, membership, metadata propagation. Efficient but eventual. Consider performance and maintainability.

System Design.expert: Requirements: mutual exclusion, fault tolerance, deadlock freedom, reentrancy. ZooKeeper: ephemeral sequential znode for lock. Etcd: leases and revision-based locking. System Design.front: What is a database connection pool and sizing?

System Design.hard: Pool caches connections for reuse avoiding connection overhead. Size formula: connections = (core_count * 2) + effective_spindle_count. Too many: database overwhelmed (context switching). Too few: requests queued. PostgreSQL: max_connections = pool_size + superuser_reserved.
System Design.expert: Pool caches connections for reuse avoiding connection overhead. Size formula: connections = (core_count * 2) + effective_spindle_count. Too many: database overwhelmed (context switching). Too few: requests queued. PostgreSQL: max_connections = pool_size + superuser_reserved. Choose based on your specific requirements.

System Design.expert: WAL records every state change before applying. On crash, replay WAL. Provides durability, atomicity. PostgreSQL: WAL for crash recovery and replication. System Design.front: What is the difference between leaderless and leader-based replication?

System Design.normal: Leader-based: one leader handles writes, replicas. Strong consistency possible. Leaderless: any node accepts writes, read. Higher availability.
System Design.hard: Leader-based: one leader handles writes, replicas follow (PostgreSQL, MySQL, Kafka). Strong consistency possible. Leaderless: any node accepts writes, read repair handles inconsistency (Cassandra, Dynamo). Higher availability but weaker consistency. Quorum reads/writes.
System Design.expert: Leader-based: one leader handles writes, replicas follow (PostgreSQL, MySQL, Kafka). Strong consistency possible. Leaderless: any node accepts writes, read repair handles inconsistency (Cassandra, Dynamo). Higher availability but weaker consistency. Quorum reads/writes. Consider performance and maintainability.

System Design.hard: Redis Sentinel: monitoring, automatic failover, primary detection. Redis Cluster: automatic sharding, replication, gossip. Memcached: simple distributed hash with consistent hashing on client side. Proxy layer: Twemproxy, Redis Enterprise for advanced routing.
System Design.expert: Redis Sentinel: monitoring, automatic failover, primary detection. Redis Cluster: automatic sharding, replication, gossip. System Design.expert: Services register their address on startup (IP:port). Heartbeats renew registration. Clients discover via registry. System Design.hard: Kimball dimensional modeling: fact tables (measures) + dimension tables (attributes). Star schema: denormalized dimensions around fact. Snowflake schema: normalized dimensions. System Design.expert: Kimball dimensional modeling: fact tables (measures) + dimension tables (attributes). Star schema: denormalized dimensions around fact. Snowflake schema: normalized dimensions. System Design.expert: Idempotency key: client generates unique key per request. Store processed keys in Redis with TTL. Compare key before processing. For stream: dedup in window via bloom filter or exact set. Watermark for event-time dedup in streaming (Flink). Choose based on your specific requirements.

System Design.expert: REST: request-response, JSON. gRPC: four types - unary (request-response), server streaming, client streaming, bidirectional streaming. gRPC uses HTTP/2 multiplexed connections, protobuf for efficient binary serialization. System Design.front: Design a system for handling webhook delivery.

System Design.expert: Webhook: HTTP callback on event. Components: webhook registration, event queue, delivery workers, retry queue, dead letter queue. System Design.hard: Publisher confirms (ack from broker), persistent messages (disk), mirrored queues (HA), consumer acknowledgements (manual ack). Dead letter exchange for failed messages. Delivery guarantees: at-most-once, at-least-once (acks), exactly-once (with dedup).
System Design.expert: Publisher confirms (ack from broker), persistent messages (disk), mirrored queues (HA), consumer acknowledgements (manual ack). Dead letter exchange for failed messages. Delivery guarantees: at-most-once, at-least-once (acks), exactly-once (with dedup). Consider performance and maintainability.

System Design.hard: Choreography: each service publishes events triggering next services compensating actions. Orchestration: coordinator directs services with commands. System Design.front: What is a hot partition and how to solve it?

System Design.hard: Hot partition: disproportionate load on one partition. Causes: skewed data distribution, popular key. Solutions: partition split (rehash), add salting (append random value to key), separate hot data, pre-split with many partitions. Cassandra: partition with limit.
System Design.expert: Hot partition: disproportionate load on one partition. Causes: skewed data distribution, popular key. Solutions: partition split (rehash), add salting (append random value to key), separate hot data, pre-split with many partitions. Cassandra: partition with limit. Context determines the best approach.

System Design.hard: Auto-sharding: distribute data across nodes (Vitess, Citus, CockroachDB). Consistent hashing or hash-based. Query routing: proxy layer routes to correct shard. Cross-shard queries: scatter-gather. Resharding: incremental migration. Transactions span shards via 2PC or XA.
System Design.expert: Auto-sharding: distribute data across nodes (Vitess, Citus, CockroachDB). Consistent hashing or hash-based. Query routing: proxy layer routes to correct shard. Cross-shard queries: scatter-gather. Resharding: incremental migration. Transactions span shards via 2PC or XA. Context determines the best approach.

System Design.hard: Fan-out on write: pre-compute timeline for each user when tweet created. Good for small number of followers. Fan-out on read: pull tweets from followees at read time. Hybrid: pre-compute for active users, pull for inactive. Redis sorted sets for timelines.

System Design.expert: Client generates idempotency key (UUID) sent in header. Server stores processed keys with response in DB with TTL. On duplicate key return cached response. System Design.expert: Bloom filter can quickly tell if a key definitely does NOT exist. Cache filtering: check bloom filter before querying cache/memcache. Security.hard: XSS injects malicious scripts into web pages viewed by others. Types: Stored (persistent in DB), Reflected (in URL/request), DOM-based (client-side). Prevention: output encoding (HTML entity encode), Content Security Policy (CSP), input validation, HttpOnly cookies.
Security.expert: XSS injects malicious scripts into web pages viewed by others. Types: Stored (persistent in DB), Reflected (in URL/request), DOM-based (client-side). Prevention: output encoding (HTML entity encode), Content Security Policy (CSP), input validation, HttpOnly cookies. Context determines the best approach.

Security.hard: CSRF tricks user into executing unwanted actions on authenticated site. Prevention: anti-CSRF tokens (synchronizer token pattern), SameSite cookies (Strict/Lax), Origin/Referer header validation, re-authentication for sensitive actions. Tokens tied to session.
Security.expert: CSRF tricks user into executing unwanted actions on authenticated site. Prevention: anti-CSRF tokens (synchronizer token pattern), SameSite cookies (Strict/Lax), Origin/Referer header validation, re-authentication for sensitive actions. Tokens tied to session. Security.expert: OAuth 2.0: Resource Owner (user) grants authorization to Client (app) via Authorization Server. Common flows: Authorization Code (server-side apps), Implicit (SPAs, deprecated), Client Credentials (machine-to-machine), PKCE for mobile/SPA. Returns access token (JWT/opaque). Security.hard: JWT (JSON Web Token): base64url-encoded header.payload.signature. Stateless auth, contains claims. Security: use strong signing (RS256/ES256), short expiration, validate signature + claims, store in httpOnly cookie not localStorage. Secret rotation. No sensitive data in payload.
Security.expert: JWT (JSON Web Token): base64url-encoded header.payload.signature. Stateless auth, contains claims. Security: use strong signing (RS256/ES256), short expiration, validate signature + claims, store in httpOnly cookie not localStorage. Secret rotation. No sensitive data in payload. Context determines the best approach.

Security.front: How does HTTPS/TLS work?
