Security.normal: TLS handshake: client sends supported ciphers. Then symmetric encryption (AES-GCM). Perfect Forward Secrecy: ephemeral Diffie-Hellman.
Security.hard: TLS handshake: client sends supported ciphers, server sends certificate (chain), client verifies CA signature, generates pre-master secret encrypted with server public key, both derive session keys. Then symmetric encryption (AES-GCM). Perfect Forward Secrecy: ephemeral Diffie-Hellman.
Security.expert: TLS handshake: client sends supported ciphers, server sends certificate (chain), client verifies CA signature, generates pre-master secret encrypted with server public key, both derive session keys. Then symmetric encryption (AES-GCM). Perfect Forward Secrecy: ephemeral Diffie-Hellman. Consider performance and maintainability.

Security.front: What is a Man-in-the-Middle (MitM) attack?
Security.easy: It helps you learn about Middle.
Security.normal: Attacker intercepts communication between two parties. Can read, modify, inject data. Prevention: TLS with certificate validation, HSTS. Risks: public WiFi, DNS spoofing, ARP.
Security.hard: Attacker intercepts communication between two parties undetected. Can read, modify, inject data. Prevention: TLS with certificate validation, HSTS, certificate pinning, mutual TLS. Risks: public WiFi, DNS spoofing, ARP poisoning.
Security.expert: Attacker intercepts communication between two parties undetected. Can read, modify, inject data. Prevention: TLS with certificate validation, HSTS, certificate pinning, mutual TLS. Risks: public WiFi, DNS spoofing, ARP poisoning. Consider performance and maintainability.

Security.front: Explain the principle of least privilege.
Security.easy: It helps you learn about principle.
Security.normal: Users/services should have minimum permissions needed. Reduces attack surface, limits blast radius. Implemented via: RBAC roles, IAM policies.
Security.hard: Users/services should have minimum permissions needed to function. Reduces attack surface, limits blast radius. Implemented via: RBAC roles, IAM policies, service accounts, network segmentation (firewall rules), container security contexts, Unix file permissions.
Security.expert: Users/services should have minimum permissions needed to function. Reduces attack surface, limits blast radius. Implemented via: RBAC roles, IAM policies, service accounts, network segmentation (firewall rules), container security contexts, Unix file permissions. Choose based on your specific requirements.

Security.front: How does a firewall work?
Security.easy: It helps you learn about firewall.
Security.normal: Firewall filters traffic based on rules. Types: packet filter stateless, stateful. Default deny: block all then allow. Network ACLs vs Security Groups (AWS).
Security.hard: Firewall filters traffic based on rules: source IP, destination IP, port, protocol. Types: packet filter (stateless), stateful (tracks connections), next-gen (application-layer inspection, IPS). Default deny: block all then allow specific. Network ACLs vs Security Groups (AWS).
Security.expert: Firewall filters traffic based on rules: source IP, destination IP, port, protocol. Types: packet filter (stateless), stateful (tracks connections), next-gen (application-layer inspection, IPS). Default deny: block all then allow specific. Network ACLs vs Security Groups (AWS). Evaluate trade-offs before deciding.

Security.front: What is defense in depth?
Security.easy: It helps you learn about defense.
Security.normal: Multiple layers of security controls. Layers: perimeter firewall, network segmentation, VPN. No single point of failure.
Security.hard: Multiple layers of security controls so if one fails another protects. Layers: perimeter (firewall), network (segmentation, VPN), host (OS hardening, antivirus), application (input validation, auth), data (encryption, access control), physical. No single point of failure.
Security.expert: Multiple layers of security controls so if one fails another protects. Layers: perimeter (firewall), network (segmentation, VPN), host (OS hardening, antivirus), application (input validation, auth), data (encryption, access control), physical. No single point of failure. Evaluate trade-offs before deciding.

Security.front: Explain common types of cryptography.
Security.easy: It helps you learn about common.
Security.normal: Symmetric: same key for encrypt/decrypt . Fast, key distribution problem. Asymmetric: public/private key pair . Slower, key exchange. Hashing: one-way (SHA-256, bcrypt, Argon2). Hybrid: TLS uses asymmetric for key.
Security.hard: Symmetric: same key for encrypt/decrypt (AES-256, ChaCha20). Fast, key distribution problem. Asymmetric: public/private key pair (RSA, ECDSA, Ed25519). Slower, key exchange. Hashing: one-way (SHA-256, bcrypt, Argon2). Hybrid: TLS uses asymmetric for key exchange then symmetric for data.
Security.expert: Symmetric: same key for encrypt/decrypt (AES-256, ChaCha20). Fast, key distribution problem. Asymmetric: public/private key pair (RSA, ECDSA, Ed25519). Slower, key exchange. Hashing: one-way (SHA-256, bcrypt, Argon2). Hybrid: TLS uses asymmetric for key exchange then symmetric for data. Consider performance and maintainability.

Security.front: What is a DDoS attack and mitigation?
Security.easy: It helps you learn about DDoS.
Security.normal: DDoS overwhelms resources with traffic. Types: volumetric bandwidth, protocol SYN flood. Mitigation: CDN/scrubbing centers, rate limiting, WAF.
Security.hard: DDoS (Distributed Denial of Service) overwhelms resources with traffic. Types: volumetric (bandwidth), protocol (SYN flood), application-layer (HTTP flood). Mitigation: CDN/scrubbing centers, rate limiting, WAF, auto-scaling, Anycast routing, cloud DDoS protection (AWS Shield, Cloudflare).
Security.expert: DDoS (Distributed Denial of Service) overwhelms resources with traffic. Types: volumetric (bandwidth), protocol (SYN flood), application-layer (HTTP flood). Mitigation: CDN/scrubbing centers, rate limiting, WAF, auto-scaling, Anycast routing, cloud DDoS protection (AWS Shield, Cloudflare). Consider performance and maintainability.

Security.front: How does a Web Application Firewall (WAF) work?
Security.easy: It helps you learn about Application.
Security.normal: WAF filters HTTP traffic between client. Detects: SQL injection, XSS, path traversal. Modes: block , detect , prevent. Rules: OWASP CRS , custom rules. Cloud WAF: AWS WAF, Cloudflare, Imperva.
Security.hard: WAF filters HTTP traffic between client and web app. Detects: SQL injection, XSS, path traversal, RFI/LFI, CSRF. Modes: block (deny), detect (log only), prevent. Rules: OWASP CRS (core rule set), custom rules. Cloud WAF: AWS WAF, Cloudflare, Imperva.
Security.expert: WAF filters HTTP traffic between client and web app. Detects: SQL injection, XSS, path traversal, RFI/LFI, CSRF. Modes: block (deny), detect (log only), prevent. Rules: OWASP CRS (core rule set), custom rules. Cloud WAF: AWS WAF, Cloudflare, Imperva. Evaluate trade-offs before deciding.

Security.front: Explain zero trust security model.
Security.easy: It helps you learn about zero.
Security.normal: Never trust, always verify. No implicit trust based on network. Requires: continuous authentication, device posture check. BeyondCorp (Google), Zscaler. Every access request authenticated and authorized.
Security.hard: Never trust, always verify. No implicit trust based on network location. Requires: continuous authentication, device posture check, micro-segmentation, least privilege, encryption everywhere. BeyondCorp (Google), Zscaler. Every access request authenticated and authorized regardless of origin.
Security.expert: Never trust, always verify. No implicit trust based on network location. Requires: continuous authentication, device posture check, micro-segmentation, least privilege, encryption everywhere. BeyondCorp (Google), Zscaler. Every access request authenticated and authorized regardless of origin. Context determines the best approach.

Security.front: What is the difference between hashing and encryption?
Security.easy: It helps you learn about difference.
Security.normal: Hashing: one-way function, fixed output, cannot. Used for passwords, integrity checks. Encryption: two-way, reversible with key  Confidentiality. Hashing is deterministic; encryption is not.
Security.hard: Hashing: one-way function, fixed output, cannot reverse (SHA-256, bcrypt). Used for passwords, integrity checks. Encryption: two-way, reversible with key (AES, RSA). Confidentiality. Hashing is deterministic; encryption is not necessarily (block cipher modes).
Security.expert: Hashing: one-way function, fixed output, cannot reverse (SHA-256, bcrypt). Used for passwords, integrity checks. Encryption: two-way, reversible with key (AES, RSA). Confidentiality. Hashing is deterministic; encryption is not necessarily (block cipher modes). Context determines the best approach.

Security.front: How does password hashing work securely?
Security.easy: It helps you learn about password.
Security.normal: Use slow adaptive hash: bcrypt Blowfish. Salt each password (unique per user). Work factor increases with hardware Storage. Compare constant-time to prevent timing attack. Never use MD5/SHA-1 for passwords.
Security.hard: Use slow adaptive hash: bcrypt (Blowfish), Argon2 (memory-hard), scrypt (CPU+memory). Salt each password (unique per user). Work factor increases with hardware. Storage: $algorithm$iterations$salt$hash. Compare constant-time to prevent timing attack. Never use MD5/SHA-1 for passwords.
Security.expert: Use slow adaptive hash: bcrypt (Blowfish), Argon2 (memory-hard), scrypt (CPU+memory). Salt each password (unique per user). Work factor increases with hardware. Storage: $algorithm$iterations$salt$hash. Compare constant-time to prevent timing attack. Never use MD5/SHA-1 for passwords. Evaluate trade-offs before deciding.

Security.front: What is a JWT access token vs refresh token?
Security.easy: It helps you learn about access.
Security.normal: Access token short-lived, 15min: sent. Refresh token long-lived, 7-30 days: used. Refresh token stored securely (httpOnly cookie). Rotation: refresh token invalidated after use.
Security.hard: Access token (short-lived, 15min): sent with each request for authorization. Refresh token (long-lived, 7-30 days): used to get new access tokens without re-authentication. Refresh token stored securely (httpOnly cookie). Rotation: refresh token invalidated after use.
Security.expert: Access token (short-lived, 15min): sent with each request for authorization. Refresh token (long-lived, 7-30 days): used to get new access tokens without re-authentication. Refresh token stored securely (httpOnly cookie). Rotation: refresh token invalidated after use. Consider performance and maintainability.

Security.front: Explain SSRF vulnerability.
Security.easy: It helps you learn about SSRF.
Security.normal: Server-Side Request Forgery: attacker makes server. Prevention: validate/whitelist URLs, block metadata IPs.
Security.hard: Server-Side Request Forgery: attacker makes server make requests to internal resources (e.g., metadata endpoints, internal services). Prevention: validate/whitelist URLs, block metadata IPs (169.254.169.254), disable unnecessary redirects, network segmentation, URL allow listing.
Security.expert: Server-Side Request Forgery: attacker makes server make requests to internal resources (e.g., metadata endpoints, internal services). Prevention: validate/whitelist URLs, block metadata IPs (169.254.169.254), disable unnecessary redirects, network segmentation, URL allow listing. Choose based on your specific requirements.

Security.front: How does a secure session management work?
Security.easy: It helps you learn about secure.
Security.normal: Session ID generated with high entropy. Session stored server-side (Redis, DB). Regenerate on login. Expire on logout/timeout. Implement absolute + idle timeouts. Prevent fixation: new session after auth.
Security.hard: Session ID generated with high entropy (CSPRNG), transmitted via httpOnly Secure SameSite cookie. Session stored server-side (Redis, DB). Regenerate on login. Expire on logout/timeout. Implement absolute + idle timeouts. Prevent fixation: new session after auth.
Security.expert: Session ID generated with high entropy (CSPRNG), transmitted via httpOnly Secure SameSite cookie. Session stored server-side (Redis, DB). Regenerate on login. Expire on logout/timeout. Implement absolute + idle timeouts. Prevent fixation: new session after auth. Choose based on your specific requirements.

Security.front: What is the difference between symmetric and asymmetric encryption?
Security.easy: It helps you learn about difference.
Security.normal: Symmetric: single key for encrypt/decrypt, fast. Key distribution challenge. Asymmetric: public/private key, slow . Used for key exchange and digital. Hybrid: asymmetric exchange symmetric key then.
Security.hard: Symmetric: single key for encrypt/decrypt, fast (AES-256, 1GB/s). Key distribution challenge. Asymmetric: public/private key, slow (RSA-4096, ~10K ops/s). Used for key exchange and digital signatures. Hybrid: asymmetric exchange symmetric key then symmetric encryption.
Security.expert: Symmetric: single key for encrypt/decrypt, fast (AES-256, 1GB/s). Key distribution challenge. Asymmetric: public/private key, slow (RSA-4096, ~10K ops/s). Used for key exchange and digital signatures. Hybrid: asymmetric exchange symmetric key then symmetric encryption. Context determines the best approach.

Security.front: Explain Content Security Policy (CSP).
Security.easy: It helps you learn about Content.
Security.normal: CSP header prevents XSS and data. Controls resources browser can load: script-src. Values: self, domain, nonce, hash, unsafe-inline. Report-URI/report-to for violation reports. Reduces impact of XSS vulnerabilities.
Security.hard: CSP header prevents XSS and data injection. Controls resources browser can load: script-src, style-src, img-src, frame-src. Values: self, domain, nonce, hash, unsafe-inline (avoid). Report-URI/report-to for violation reports. Reduces impact of XSS vulnerabilities.
Security.expert: CSP header prevents XSS and data injection. Controls resources browser can load: script-src, style-src, img-src, frame-src. Values: self, domain, nonce, hash, unsafe-inline (avoid). Report-URI/report-to for violation reports. Reduces impact of XSS vulnerabilities. Context determines the best approach.

Security.front: What is IDOR (Insecure Direct Object Reference)?
Security.easy: It helps you learn about IDOR.
Security.normal: IDOR: attacker accesses unauthorized object. Prevention: authorization check for every object.
Security.hard: IDOR: attacker accesses unauthorized object by modifying identifier (e.g., /user/123 -> /user/124). Prevention: authorization check for every object access, use GUIDs/UUIDs instead of sequential IDs, indirect reference maps (OWASP ESAPI AccessReferenceMap).
Security.expert: IDOR: attacker accesses unauthorized object by modifying identifier (e.g., /user/123 -> /user/124). Prevention: authorization check for every object access, use GUIDs/UUIDs instead of sequential IDs, indirect reference maps (OWASP ESAPI AccessReferenceMap). Evaluate trade-offs before deciding.

Security.front: How does a security audit log work?
Security.easy: It helps you learn about security.
Security.normal: Audit log records security-relevant events: authentication. Requirements: tamper-proof immutable storage, timestamp NTP-synced. SIEM systems aggregate and alert.
Security.hard: Audit log records security-relevant events: authentication attempts, access control changes, data modifications, privilege escalation. Requirements: tamper-proof (immutable storage), timestamp (NTP-synced), user identification, event categorization. SIEM systems (Splunk, ELK) aggregate and alert.
Security.expert: Audit log records security-relevant events: authentication attempts, access control changes, data modifications, privilege escalation. Requirements: tamper-proof (immutable storage), timestamp (NTP-synced), user identification, event categorization. SIEM systems (Splunk, ELK) aggregate and alert. Choose based on your specific requirements.

Security.front: Explain the concept of a security onion model.
Security.easy: It helps you learn about concept.
Security.normal: Defense in depth with detection layers. Each layer provides detection opportunity. Tools: Security Onion distro integrates multiple.
Security.hard: Defense in depth with detection layers: network IDS (Snort/Suricata), host IDS (Osquery/Wazuh), log analysis, threat intelligence, file integrity monitoring (Tripwire), honeypots. Each layer provides detection opportunity. Tools: Security Onion distro integrates multiple layers.
Security.expert: Defense in depth with detection layers: network IDS (Snort/Suricata), host IDS (Osquery/Wazuh), log analysis, threat intelligence, file integrity monitoring (Tripwire), honeypots. Each layer provides detection opportunity. Tools: Security Onion distro integrates multiple layers. Consider performance and maintainability.

Security.front: What is a buffer overflow and mitigation?
Security.easy: It helps you learn about buffer.
Security.normal: Buffer overflow: writing data beyond buffer. Exploits: overwrite return address for code. Mitigations: ASLR address randomization, NX.
Security.hard: Buffer overflow: writing data beyond buffer bounds overwriting adjacent memory. Exploits: overwrite return address for code execution. Mitigations: ASLR (address randomization), NX (non-executable stack), stack canaries, safe languages (Rust, Go), bounds checking, W xor X.
Security.expert: Buffer overflow: writing data beyond buffer bounds overwriting adjacent memory. Exploits: overwrite return address for code execution. Mitigations: ASLR (address randomization), NX (non-executable stack), stack canaries, safe languages (Rust, Go), bounds checking, W xor X. Choose based on your specific requirements.

Security.front: How does a certificate authority (CA) work?
Security.easy: It helps you learn about certificate.
Security.normal: CA issues digital certificates binding public. CA verifies identity DV, OV, EV. Browsers trust CAs via root store. Certificate chain: root -> intermediate ->. Revocation: CRL, OCSP. Let's Encrypt automates DV issuance.
Security.hard: CA issues digital certificates binding public key to identity. CA verifies identity (DV, OV, EV) then signs certificate with its private key. Browsers trust CAs via root store. Certificate chain: root -> intermediate -> server. Revocation: CRL, OCSP. Let's Encrypt automates DV issuance.
Security.expert: CA issues digital certificates binding public key to identity. CA verifies identity (DV, OV, EV) then signs certificate with its private key. Browsers trust CAs via root store. Certificate chain: root -> intermediate -> server. Revocation: CRL, OCSP. Let's Encrypt automates DV issuance. Context determines the best approach.

Security.front: What is a path traversal attack?
Security.easy: It helps you learn about path.
Security.normal: Path traversal: ../ sequences to access. Prevention: normalize paths, reject ../ patterns. Use whitelist of allowed file names.
Security.hard: Path traversal: ../ sequences to access files outside web root (../../../etc/passwd). Prevention: normalize paths, reject ../ patterns, use chroot/jail, serve files from restricted directory, avoid user input in file paths. Use whitelist of allowed file names.
Security.expert: Path traversal: ../ sequences to access files outside web root (../../../etc/passwd). Prevention: normalize paths, reject ../ patterns, use chroot/jail, serve files from restricted directory, avoid user input in file paths. Use whitelist of allowed file names. Choose based on your specific requirements.

Security.front: Explain the difference between authN and authZ in APIs.
Security.easy: It helps you learn about difference.
Security.normal: AuthN authentication: verify identity via API. AuthZ authorization: check permissions via scopes. Middleware: first authenticate, then authorize. JWT carries both identity sub.
Security.hard: AuthN (authentication): verify identity via API key, JWT, OAuth2 token. AuthZ (authorization): check permissions via scopes, roles, claims. Middleware: first authenticate, then authorize. JWT carries both identity (sub) and permissions (scope). gRPC uses interceptors for both.
Security.expert: AuthN (authentication): verify identity via API key, JWT, OAuth2 token. AuthZ (authorization): check permissions via scopes, roles, claims. Middleware: first authenticate, then authorize. JWT carries both identity (sub) and permissions (scope). gRPC uses interceptors for both. Consider performance and maintainability.

Security.front: How does security key (FIDO2/WebAuthn) work?
Security.easy: It helps you learn about security.
Security.normal: User registers public key with service. Authentication: service sends challenge, user signs. No shared secrets, phishing-resistant. WebAuthn browser API. User verification: PIN, biometric. Passkeys extend this for cross-device sync.
Security.hard: User registers public key with service. Authentication: service sends challenge, user signs with private key (on hardware key). No shared secrets, phishing-resistant. WebAuthn browser API. User verification: PIN, biometric. Passkeys extend this for cross-device sync.
Security.expert: User registers public key with service. Authentication: service sends challenge, user signs with private key (on hardware key). No shared secrets, phishing-resistant. WebAuthn browser API. User verification: PIN, biometric. Passkeys extend this for cross-device sync. Consider performance and maintainability.

Security.front: What is a side-channel attack?
Security.easy: It helps you learn about side.
Security.normal: Side-channel attacks exploit physical information: timing. Mitigations: constant-time algorithms, blinding, noise injection.
Security.hard: Side-channel attacks exploit physical information: timing (how long operation takes), power analysis (power consumption), electromagnetic emissions, cache timing (Spectre/Meltdown), acoustic. Mitigations: constant-time algorithms, blinding, noise injection, data-independent memory access patterns.
Security.expert: Side-channel attacks exploit physical information: timing (how long operation takes), power analysis (power consumption), electromagnetic emissions, cache timing (Spectre/Meltdown), acoustic. Mitigations: constant-time algorithms, blinding, noise injection, data-independent memory access patterns. Context determines the best approach.

Security.front: Explain the CIA triad.
Security.easy: It helps you learn about triad.
Security.normal: Confidentiality: data accessible only to authorized. Integrity: data not tampered . Availability: system accessible when needed . Security controls often address multiple triad.
Security.hard: Confidentiality: data accessible only to authorized (encryption, access control). Integrity: data not tampered (hashing, digital signatures, checksums). Availability: system accessible when needed (redundancy, backups, DDoS mitigation). Security controls often address multiple triad elements.
Security.expert: Confidentiality: data accessible only to authorized (encryption, access control). Integrity: data not tampered (hashing, digital signatures, checksums). Availability: system accessible when needed (redundancy, backups, DDoS mitigation). Security controls often address multiple triad elements. Context determines the best approach.

Security.front: How does encryption at rest vs in transit differ?
Security.easy: It helps you learn about encryption.
Security.normal: At rest: encrypt stored data AES-256. In transit: encrypt network traffic . Both needed for defense in depth. Key management: HSM, KMS .
Security.hard: At rest: encrypt stored data (AES-256) via disk encryption (LUKS, BitLocker), DB encryption (TDE), object encryption (S3 SSE). In transit: encrypt network traffic (TLS, mTLS, SSH). Both needed for defense in depth. Key management: HSM, KMS (AWS KMS, HashiCorp Vault).
Security.expert: At rest: encrypt stored data (AES-256) via disk encryption (LUKS, BitLocker), DB encryption (TDE), object encryption (S3 SSE). In transit: encrypt network traffic (TLS, mTLS, SSH). Both needed for defense in depth. Key management: HSM, KMS (AWS KMS, HashiCorp Vault). Context determines the best approach.

Security.front: What is a social engineering attack?
Security.easy: It helps you learn about social.
Security.normal: Manipulating people into revealing confidential information. Types: phishing email, spear phishing targeted. Prevention: security awareness training, MFA, verify.
Security.hard: Manipulating people into revealing confidential information. Types: phishing (email), spear phishing (targeted), pretexting (fabricated scenario), baiting (USB drops), tailgating (following authorized person). Prevention: security awareness training, MFA, verify requests via separate channel.
Security.expert: Manipulating people into revealing confidential information. Types: phishing (email), spear phishing (targeted), pretexting (fabricated scenario), baiting (USB drops), tailgating (following authorized person). Prevention: security awareness training, MFA, verify requests via separate channel. Consider performance and maintainability.

Security.front: Explain the STRIDE threat model.
Security.easy: It helps you learn about STRIDE.
Security.normal: Microsofts threat categorization: Spoofing fake identity. Each maps to security control: AuthN.
Security.hard: Microsofts threat categorization: Spoofing (fake identity), Tampering (modify data), Repudiation (deny action), Information Disclosure (data leak), Denial of Service, Elevation of Privilege. Each maps to security control: AuthN, Integrity, Audit, Confidentiality, Availability, AuthZ.
Security.expert: Microsofts threat categorization: Spoofing (fake identity), Tampering (modify data), Repudiation (deny action), Information Disclosure (data leak), Denial of Service, Elevation of Privilege. Each maps to security control: AuthN, Integrity, Audit, Confidentiality, Availability, AuthZ. Evaluate trade-offs before deciding.

Security.front: How does a Hardware Security Module (HSM) work?
Security.easy: It helps you learn about Hardware.
Security.normal: HSM is tamper-resistant hardware that safely. Keys never leave HSM in plaintext. Accelerates cryptographic operations. FIPS 140-2/3 certified. Used for: PKI, code signing, database.
Security.hard: HSM is tamper-resistant hardware that safely generates, stores, and manages cryptographic keys. Keys never leave HSM in plaintext. Accelerates cryptographic operations. FIPS 140-2/3 certified. Used for: PKI, code signing, database encryption (TDE), payment processing (PCI-HSM).
Security.expert: HSM is tamper-resistant hardware that safely generates, stores, and manages cryptographic keys. Keys never leave HSM in plaintext. Accelerates cryptographic operations. FIPS 140-2/3 certified. Used for: PKI, code signing, database encryption (TDE), payment processing (PCI-HSM). Evaluate trade-offs before deciding.

Security.front: What is OWASP Top 10?
Security.easy: It helps you learn about OWASP.
Security.normal: List of most critical web app. 2021: A01 Broken Access Control, A02.
Security.hard: List of most critical web app security risks. 2021: A01 Broken Access Control, A02 Cryptographic Failures, A03 Injection, A04 Insecure Design, A05 Security Misconfiguration, A06 Vulnerable Components, A07 Auth Failures, A08 Software/Data Integrity, A09 Logging Failures, A10 SSRF.
Security.expert: List of most critical web app security risks. 2021: A01 Broken Access Control, A02 Cryptographic Failures, A03 Injection, A04 Insecure Design, A05 Security Misconfiguration, A06 Vulnerable Components, A07 Auth Failures, A08 Software/Data Integrity, A09 Logging Failures, A10 SSRF. Choose based on your specific requirements.

Security.front: Explain how to secure a REST API.
Security.easy: It helps you learn about secure.
Security.normal: Use HTTPS always. Auth: OAuth2/OpenID Connect or API keys. Validate all inputs (schema, type, length). Rate limiting per user/IP. CORS strict configuration. No sensitive data in URLs Audit. Response headers: CSP, X-Frame-Options, X-Content-Type-Options.
Security.hard: Use HTTPS always. Auth: OAuth2/OpenID Connect or API keys with scopes. Validate all inputs (schema, type, length). Rate limiting per user/IP. CORS strict configuration. No sensitive data in URLs. Audit logging. Response headers: CSP, X-Frame-Options, X-Content-Type-Options.
Security.expert: Use HTTPS always. Auth: OAuth2/OpenID Connect or API keys with scopes. Validate all inputs (schema, type, length). Rate limiting per user/IP. CORS strict configuration. No sensitive data in URLs. Audit logging. Response headers: CSP, X-Frame-Options, X-Content-Type-Options. Evaluate trade-offs before deciding.

Security.front: What is supply chain security?
Security.easy: It helps you learn about supply.
Security.normal: Vulnerabilities from third-party dependencies, compromised build. Mitigations: software bill of materials SBOM.
Security.hard: Vulnerabilities from third-party dependencies, compromised build tools, malicious packages. Mitigations: software bill of materials (SBOM), dependency scanning (Dependabot, Snyk), lock files (package-lock.json), pin versions, signed commits, reproducible builds, container image scanning.
Security.expert: Vulnerabilities from third-party dependencies, compromised build tools, malicious packages. Mitigations: software bill of materials (SBOM), dependency scanning (Dependabot, Snyk), lock files (package-lock.json), pin versions, signed commits, reproducible builds, container image scanning. Context determines the best approach.

Security.front: How does Docker container security work?
Security.easy: It helps you learn about Docker.
Security.normal: Container isolation via kernel namespaces . Run as non-root user, read-only root. Image scanning for vulnerabilities. Not root on host: user namespace.
Security.hard: Container isolation via kernel namespaces (cgroups, pid, net, mnt). Run as non-root user, read-only root filesystem, drop capabilities (--cap-drop ALL), seccomp profiles, AppArmor/SELinux. Image scanning for vulnerabilities. Not root on host: user namespace remapping.
Security.expert: Container isolation via kernel namespaces (cgroups, pid, net, mnt). Run as non-root user, read-only root filesystem, drop capabilities (--cap-drop ALL), seccomp profiles, AppArmor/SELinux. Image scanning for vulnerabilities. Not root on host: user namespace remapping. Choose based on your specific requirements.

Security.front: Explain the difference between black-box and white-box testing.
Security.easy: It helps you learn about difference.
Security.normal: Black-box: tester has no internal knowledge. White-box: full access to source code. Grey-box: partial knowledge. Penetration tests often combine approaches.
Security.hard: Black-box: tester has no internal knowledge, tests from user perspective (pen testing, fuzzing). White-box: full access to source code, architecture diagrams (code review, SAST). Grey-box: partial knowledge. Penetration tests often combine approaches.
Security.expert: Black-box: tester has no internal knowledge, tests from user perspective (pen testing, fuzzing). White-box: full access to source code, architecture diagrams (code review, SAST). Grey-box: partial knowledge. Penetration tests often combine approaches. Choose based on your specific requirements.

Security.front: What is a DDoS mitigation strategy using rate limiting?
Security.easy: It helps you learn about DDoS.
Security.normal: Rate limit per IP, per user. Token bucket or sliding window. Application-layer: challenge for suspicious traffic. Network-layer: blackhole/null route, BGP Flowspec. CDN absorbs at edge. Auto-scaling absorbs traffic bursts.
Security.hard: Rate limit per IP, per user, per endpoint. Token bucket or sliding window. Application-layer: challenge (CAPTCHA, JS challenge) for suspicious traffic. Network-layer: blackhole/null route, BGP Flowspec. CDN absorbs at edge. Auto-scaling absorbs traffic bursts.
Security.expert: Rate limit per IP, per user, per endpoint. Token bucket or sliding window. Application-layer: challenge (CAPTCHA, JS challenge) for suspicious traffic. Network-layer: blackhole/null route, BGP Flowspec. CDN absorbs at edge. Auto-scaling absorbs traffic bursts. Context determines the best approach.

Security.front: How does cryptographic signing work?
Security.easy: It helps you learn about cryptographic.
Security.normal: Signer creates hash of message, encrypts. Verifier decrypts signature with public key. Provides: authentication , integrity , non-repudiation. Used in JWTs, software signing, blockchain.
Security.hard: Signer creates hash of message, encrypts hash with private key (signature). Verifier decrypts signature with public key, compares hash. Provides: authentication (signer identity), integrity (hash mismatch detects tampering), non-repudiation. Used in JWTs, software signing, blockchain.
Security.expert: Signer creates hash of message, encrypts hash with private key (signature). Verifier decrypts signature with public key, compares hash. Provides: authentication (signer identity), integrity (hash mismatch detects tampering), non-repudiation. Used in JWTs, software signing, blockchain. Evaluate trade-offs before deciding.

Security.front: What is a session hijacking and prevention?
